title: El Niño and La Niña
what: The state of the tropical Pacific each month since 1950, as NOAA's two indices measure it: the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), NOAA's official index since February 2026, and the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), the official one before it. Both follow the sea surface temperature of the Niño 3.4 region of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific (5°N–5°S, 120°–170°W); an El Niño is five overlapping three-month seasons at or above +0.5 °C, a La Niña five at or below −0.5 °C. RONI takes away the warming of the whole tropical ocean, which ONI counts: so since the 2010s the two disagree more often. RONI names La Niñas in 2024–25 and 2025–26 that ONI does not, and ONI an El Niño in 2019–20 that RONI does not. Neither is picked. On the globe, from September 1981, the month's sea surface temperature against that month's mean over 1991–2020 (NOAA OISST): an El Niño shows as a warm tongue along the equator from South America, a La Niña as a cool one.
how: Each index is a three-month running mean; the site places each season at its middle month (December–February at January) and finds the episodes by NOAA's rule, on each value rounded to a tenth as NOAA's tables print it. The last two months are marked provisional: NOAA revises them as later measurements come in. The globe's map is OISST's monthly mean, averaged from its 0.25° grid onto the site's 1° grid, less the same calendar month's mean over 1991–2020, RONI's base period: so it shows the whole ocean's warming too, which RONI takes away and the map does not. Its colours run from blue at −4 °C through pale at no change to red at +4 °C, clipped beyond; the further from normal, the more opaque. The last month is built from preliminary days, which NOAA replaces about two weeks on. Picked instead of the sea, the globe shows what El Niño or La Niña usually does to rain (GPCP, 1979–2025) or temperature (Berkeley Earth, 1950–2024) in December–February or June–August, by either index: the mean, over the seasons the index names El Niño or La Niña (by the season's middle month, as NOAA places its seasons), of each place's departure from its own linear trend, so the warming does not read as El Niño. Where Student's t says the mean does not differ from none at 10%, it is faded. It rests on few seasons, a dozen to thirty, and the panel says how many and which; RONI's and ONI's lists of seasons differ, so their maps do. Rain runs from brown (drier) to green (wetter), never on the temperature scale; temperature from blue to red. Before 1950, when NOAA publishes no index, the site computes RONI itself by NOAA's method from two reconstructions of the sea: NOAA's ERSST v6 (from 1854) and the Met Office's HadISST (from 1870). Done the same way for 1950–2026, ERSST's matches NOAA's published RONI to 0.03 °C (root mean square). Both find the great El Niños of 1876–78 and 1887–89; they part most before 1900, when ships were few. The globe's sea before September 1981 is ERSST's, on its own 2° grid, coarser and, in the early decades, much sparser in what it rests on.
others: Other agencies use other rules. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology also measures Niño 3.4 against the tropics since September 2025, but needs ±0.8 °C and the atmosphere to respond (the Southern Oscillation Index, the pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin) before it declares an event: so it declares fewer. Its list of past events names the 2015–16 El Niño but nothing in 2014–15, when both of NOAA's indices already had El Niño, and nothing in 2018–19, when both had a weak one.
